subject: Pharmacology
vignette: In a physiology experiment, a healthy volunteer receives an infusion of a highly selective beta-1 adrenergic agonist while cardiovascular and renal parameters are monitored.
question: Which of the following effects is expected from beta-1 receptor activation?

options.text: Bronchodilation
Increased insulin secretion from the pancreas
Increased renin secretion from the kidney
Decreased salivary secretion
Vasoconstriction of vascular smooth muscle

explanation_correct: Beta-1 receptors are located in the heart (increasing heart rate and contractility) and in the kidney (increasing renin secretion). Beta-1 activation of juxtaglomerular cells raises renin release, which feeds into the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis, explaining why beta-1 blockade lowers blood pressure.

explanation_incorrect.A: Bronchodilation is a beta-2 effect on bronchial smooth muscle, not beta-1.
explanation_incorrect.B: Stimulation of insulin secretion from the pancreas is a beta-2 effect; alpha-2 activation instead inhibits insulin secretion.
explanation_incorrect.D: Decreased salivary secretion is an alpha-2 effect on salivary glands, not a beta-1 effect.
explanation_incorrect.E: Vasoconstriction of vascular smooth muscle is an alpha-1 effect; arterial smooth muscle responds to beta-2 with vasodilation.

educationalObjective: Localize beta-1 receptors to the heart (rate, contractility) and kidney (renin secretion).

subject: Pharmacology
vignette: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes enrolls in a study of an experimental drug that selectively stimulates alpha-2 adrenergic receptors on pancreatic cells. His blood glucose monitoring is intensified for the trial.
question: Which effect on insulin secretion is expected from alpha-2 activation, and which receptor subtype produces the opposite effect?

options.text: Increased insulin secretion via beta-2 receptors
Increased insulin secretion via alpha-2 receptors
No change, because alpha-2 receptors are not found in the pancreas
Decreased insulin secretion via beta-3 receptors
Decreased insulin secretion via alpha-2 receptors

explanation_correct: Alpha-2 receptors are located in the pancreas, presynaptic nerve terminals, and salivary glands. In the pancreas, alpha-2 activation inhibits insulin secretion, which can worsen hyperglycemia. The opposite effect, stimulation of insulin secretion, is mediated by beta-2 receptors on pancreatic cells, making the alpha-2/beta-2 pairing a classic contrast.

explanation_incorrect.A: This reverses both elements: alpha-2 activation decreases insulin secretion, and beta-2 (not alpha-2) activation increases it.
explanation_incorrect.B: Alpha-2 receptors inhibit rather than stimulate insulin secretion; stimulation is a beta-2 effect.
explanation_incorrect.C: Alpha-2 receptors are indeed found in the pancreas, where they inhibit insulin secretion.
explanation_incorrect.D: Beta-3 receptors are found in adipose tissue promoting lipolysis, not in pancreatic regulation of insulin secretion; the decreased secretion is an alpha-2 effect.

educationalObjective: Contrast alpha-2-mediated inhibition of insulin secretion with beta-2-mediated stimulation.

subject: Pharmacology
vignette: A researcher administers a highly selective beta-2 adrenergic agonist systemically to a study subject and records respiratory, cardiovascular, metabolic, and pancreatic responses.
question: Which combination of effects is expected from systemic beta-2 receptor activation?

options.text: Vasoconstriction, hepatic glycogenolysis, and decreased insulin secretion
Bronchodilation, arterial vasodilation, hepatic glycogenolysis, and increased insulin secretion
Increased renin secretion, bronchodilation, and vasoconstriction
Decreased heart rate, bronchodilation, and decreased blood glucose
Increased salivary secretion and contraction of the bladder detrusor

explanation_correct: Beta-2 receptors are distributed to bronchioles (bronchodilation), arterial smooth muscle (vasodilation), liver (glycogenolysis with glucose release), pancreas (stimulation of insulin secretion), and cardiac muscle (increased heart rate and contractility). A pure beta-2 agonist would therefore combine airway and vascular relaxation with hepatic glucose output and increased insulin.

explanation_incorrect.A: Vasoconstriction and decreased insulin secretion are alpha-1 and alpha-2 effects respectively; beta-2 produces vasodilation and increased insulin secretion.
explanation_incorrect.C: Increased renin secretion is a beta-1 effect on the kidney, and vasoconstriction is an alpha-1 effect; beta-2 causes vasodilation.
explanation_incorrect.D: Beta-2 activation does not decrease heart rate (it increases heart rate and contractility via cardiac beta-2 receptors) and raises, not lowers, blood glucose through glycogenolysis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Increased salivary secretion is not an adrenergic effect (alpha-2 decreases salivary secretion), and detrusor contraction is an M3 effect; beta-3 relaxes the detrusor.

educationalObjective: Recall the beta-2 tissue distribution: bronchioles, arterial smooth muscle, liver, pancreas, and cardiac muscle.

subject: Pharmacology
vignette: A 38-year-old man receives a pure alpha-1 adrenergic agonist in a research setting, and a full set of physiologic responses is recorded.
question: Which set of effects follows from alpha-1 receptor activation in its target tissues?

options.text: Vascular smooth muscle vasoconstriction, mydriasis, and contraction of intestinal and bladder sphincters
Bronchodilation, uterine relaxation (tocolysis), and increased aqueous humor production
Decreased sympathetic outflow, decreased insulin release, and increased platelet aggregation
Increased heart rate and contractility with increased renin release
Increased lipolysis with relaxation of the bladder

explanation_correct: Alpha-1 activation causes contraction of vascular smooth muscle (vasoconstriction), the pupillary dilator muscle (mydriasis), and intestinal and bladder sphincter muscles, producing urine and fecal retention during stress. These Gq-mediated contractile effects define the alpha-1 tissue profile.

explanation_incorrect.B: Bronchodilation, tocolysis, and increased aqueous humor production are beta-2 effects; alpha-1 would cause contraction rather than relaxation in those tissues.
explanation_incorrect.C: These are alpha-2 effects (decreased adrenergic outflow, decreased insulin release, increased platelet aggregation), not alpha-1 effects.
explanation_incorrect.D: Increased heart rate, contractility, and renin release are beta-1 effects on the heart and kidney.
explanation_incorrect.E: Increased lipolysis and bladder relaxation are beta-3 effects in adipose tissue and bladder.

educationalObjective: Associate alpha-1 activation with vasoconstriction, mydriasis, and sphincter contraction.
